cover.artAlt: A monarch butterfly resting on an orange flower with its wings open wide
cover.blurb: The smallest animals in the garden do the strangest things. One of them even rebuilds its whole body. Turn the page.

pages.title: Eat, Grow, Repeat
pages.artAlt: Close up of a fuzzy striped caterpillar chewing a hole in a green leaf

facts.text: A caterpillar has one job, and that job is eating. It chews leaves nearly all day and grows so fast that in about two weeks it can go from shorter than a grain of rice to about the length of your finger.

Caterpillar skin does not stretch much, so growing means climbing right out of it. A caterpillar wriggles free of its old skin around five times before it is full size. Each stage in between has its own name, an instar.
facts.artAlt: A striped monarch caterpillar halfway out of its old skin on a milkweed leaf, the wrinkled empty skin still stuck to the leaf behind it
facts.caption: Climbing out of a skin that got too small.

facts.text: The old skin does not go to waste either. Once a caterpillar has shed it, it usually turns around and eats it before going back to the leaf.
facts.artAlt: A striped caterpillar curled back on itself, chewing the crumpled old skin it has just wriggled out of
facts.caption: Nothing goes to waste: the old skin is a snack.

infographic.title: How much does a caterpillar grow?

rows.label: A monarch caterpillar the day it hatches
rows.display: about a tenth of an inch

rows.label: A full grown monarch caterpillar
rows.display: up to about 1 and three quarter inches

infographic.caption: Both caterpillar sizes come from the Monarch Joint Venture, which also says a caterpillar ends up almost 2,000 times heavier than the day it hatched. The rice and the finger are everyday sizes, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: The Great Rebuild
pages.artAlt: A see through chrysalis hanging from a stem with butterfly wing patterns showing inside

facts.text: When a caterpillar has finished growing it finds a quiet spot, hangs upside down, and splits its skin one last time. What is underneath is not a caterpillar any more. It is a chrysalis, a smooth case with a butterfly being built inside.

Inside, the body is rearranged from the inside out. That change is called metamorphosis. Wings grow, flight muscles form, and even the mouth is rebuilt, because a caterpillar chews leaves but a butterfly sips nectar through a long curled straw.
facts.artAlt: A smooth green monarch chrysalis hanging from a twig, ringed with a line of tiny gold dots
facts.caption: Still on the outside, a whole rebuild inside.

facts.text: Right at the end you can see the finished wings through the case, pattern and colors and all, because the color only arrives in the last day or two. Soon after that the butterfly climbs out and pumps fluid into its crumpled wings until they are stiff enough to fly.
facts.artAlt: A just hatched monarch butterfly gripping its empty see through case, its wings still small and crumpled
facts.caption: Just out, with wings still crumpled and soft.

infographic.title: How long does each part take?

rows.label: An egg on a milkweed leaf

infographic.caption: All three lengths of time come from the Monarch Joint Venture, and all three are summer times. A warm week makes every part quicker and a cool one slower.

pages.title: A Bee Wearing Yellow Dust
pages.artAlt: A honeybee dusted all over with yellow pollen sitting on a purple flower

facts.text: A bee is fuzzy for a reason. Pollen, the yellow dust in the middle of a flower, sticks all over those tiny hairs while the bee is busy drinking nectar. The bee then combs the dust down into little baskets on its back legs, called corbiculae, and carries it home.

As the bee bumbles from flower to flower it drops some of that pollen off, and that is pollination. It is how a plant makes seeds and fruit. About one bite in every three of the food you eat, apples, blueberries, melons, even chocolate, is there because a pollinator visited a flower first.
facts.artAlt: A honeybee standing in the middle of a white apple blossom, with small green apples growing on the branch behind it
facts.caption: Visit a blossom, and later there is an apple.

facts.text: Most bees in the world live alone, but honeybees are famous for the opposite. They share one big nest, the hive, where a single queen lays the eggs and thousands of workers fetch food and look after the young.
facts.artAlt: Hundreds of honeybees crowded over a wax honeycomb inside a hive, with the longer queen bee in the middle of them
facts.caption: One queen, thousands of workers, one busy hive.

infographic.title: How a bee turns a flower into your dinner

stops.label: Yellow pollen dust sticks all over the bee's fuzzy hairs while she drinks nectar
Some of that dust brushes off on the next flower she lands on, and that is pollination
Now that flower can make seeds, and seeds are how you get fruit
About one bite in every three that you eat began with a pollinator at a flower

infographic.caption: The one bite in every three comes from the US Department of Agriculture. The rest of the chart is the trip a single speck of pollen takes.

pages.title: The Ants Who Grow a Garden
pages.artAlt: A line of ants marching along carrying cut green pieces of leaf above their heads

facts.text: Leafcutter ants snip pieces out of leaves and carry them home along a trail, held up like green sails. Some pieces are so big for the ant that it would be like you carrying a dining table down the street, over your head, the whole way.

Here is the surprise: they do not eat the leaves. Underground they chew them into a mush and grow a fungus on it, like a farmer with a vegetable patch, and that fungus is what the ants and their babies actually eat.
facts.artAlt: A pale gray white fungus garden inside a leafcutter nest, spongy like a sponge, with small ants moving over it
facts.caption: The underground garden the ants actually eat.

facts.text: One leafcutter nest can hold three or four million ants in thousands of little underground rooms, and everybody has a job. Some cut, some carry, some tend the garden, and very tiny ants ride along on the leaf pieces as lookouts for the carriers.
facts.artAlt: A close view of one leafcutter ant holding a green leaf piece over its head, with a much tinier ant riding on top of the leaf
facts.caption: A tiny lookout hitches a ride on the leaf.

infographic.title: How long is an ant highway?

rows.label: A football field, end zone to end zone

infographic.caption: The trail comes from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, which has measured leafcutter trails longer than 2,000 feet, kept clear for months. The bus and the football field are everyday sizes, here only so you have something to measure against.
